---
title: "`Copy`, `Clone`, `Drop`: Three Different Ideas"
description: "One Rust language concept taught with one short runnable example and a precise explanation."
---

## The question

**Why can an integer still be used after assignment, but a String cannot?**

`Copy` makes an implicit bitwise value copy for eligible types; `Clone` is an explicit operation that may allocate; `Drop` is the cleanup hook called when an owned value leaves scope.

## The rule to remember

Copying a handle and cloning the owned contents are not automatically the same operation.

## The smallest complete example

Paste into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`. The [Rust examples page](examples/index.qmd) describes how to check all snippets automatically.

~~~rust
fn main() {
    let x = 3;
    let y = x; // i32 is Copy
    let a = String::from("hi");
    let b = a.clone(); // another owned String
    println!("{x} {y} {a} {b}"); // 3 3 hi hi
}
~~~

**Follow the state:** `x` remains usable because `i32` implements `Copy`. `a.clone()` requests a new String allocation, so both `a` and `b` remain valid. A normal `let b = a;` without `.clone()` would move the String instead.

## Important limitation

Types that implement `Drop` cannot also be `Copy`. `Rc::clone()` normally increments a count instead of deep-copying its inner value; inspect what a particular type's `Clone` implementation actually promises.
